Selected work

Seven systems. The first three were delivered to CERN; the rest are the infrastructure and instruments that made them possible — plus the backup system protecting the one who builds them.

  1. Agentic hardware verification

    UVMStack / AVA

    An agentic system that turns RTL and design intent into a reviewable UVM verification workflow — test plan, coverage plan, testbench — with human sign‑off gates enforced as exit codes, not good intentions.

    Role
    Architecture, engine, agent orchestration, delivery
    Stack
    Python ≥3.11 · TypeScript · Electron/React · SystemVerilog · Jinja2 · openpyxl · pyslang
    Scale
    — LOC across — files, — commits
    Delivered
    CERN AI Gateway, two desktop builds, 1,935 frontend tests passing

    What makes it hold up

    • Reproducibility is the product. Every run emits a commit‑ready bundle: the generated .sv, the plan workbook, a trajectory of every LLM and tool call with hashes, and a manifest pinning model version, skill‑pack SHA, simulator version and seed, RTL hash, spec hash, plan hash and final coverage.
    • Three pluggable layers. Agent, model and simulation backend are each a Python Protocol with multiple implementations, pinned in the run manifest so a replay reconstructs the exact stack.
    • Failure is loud. No silent degradation: every failure path re‑raises with context or names itself on stderr. Any loop over paid calls persists each unit the moment it completes, so a crash costs the in‑flight unit and nothing else.
    • Two testbench dialects. init‑tb --style uvm and --style sv share one input‑preparation path, so the two styles cannot disagree about ports, roles or plan content.

  2. Gateway repair proxy

    Haelo

    A small OpenAI‑compatible proxy that sits between the engine and any OpenAI‑compatible gateway. The engine does not change: it talks to the proxy exactly as it would talk to the gateway.

    Role
    Design and implementation
    Stack
    Python standard library only · zero dependencies · MIT
    Scale
    — LOC in — modules
    Status
    Proprietary · trial licence · 0.1.0

    What it does

    • Pins sampling to temperature 0 and fits each request to the model's actual context window.
    • Repairs schema‑invalid answers by re‑sending the failed turn as a continuation carrying the validation errors, rather than restarting.
    • Runs the engine's own hard checks and keeps long calls alive past the client's silence timeout.
    • Layer‑0 control strings per model — r‑bare, clamp‑full, lift=N, salvage, chk‑gate — measured per gateway, not guessed.

    In the AssertLLM‑mini run, Haelo took 9 of 9 designs through plan and coverage where the bare engine managed 8 of 9 on the same gateway — and with the 4K thinking cap, pairing passed plan and coverage where the uncapped run produced no answer at all after ~40 minutes.

  3. Evaluation harness

    Oden Flow

    The runtime that decides whether a model can actually do the job: a frozen benchmark tree, a SHA‑256 integrity manifest checked before every stage, and a gate loop that refuses to let a model skip a step.

    Role
    Architecture and implementation
    Stack
    Python · stdlib HTTP adapter · systemd user units · local model serving
    Scale
    — LOC in — files, — commits
    Coverage
    3 task sets · 6 / 9 / 18 DUTs · 7 benchmark suites

    The rules it enforces

    • Nothing is patched. The engine and benchmark tree are deployed verbatim; a SHA‑256 manifest is taken at deploy time and verified before every stage. A difference is a refusal, not a warning.
    • Same items, same conditions. One canonical order frozen for the whole campaign, lockstep blocks of ten, identical prompts, temperature 0, and context‑exceeded counted as an attempted failure so the denominator never shifts.
    • Stop at the first bad step. A failed step ends that model's round — the remainder will not build well on a bad base. Steps that passed are kept and never redone.
    • Infrastructure failures are not model failures. Calls the adapter marked as infrastructure faults are re‑run rather than charged to the model.

  4. Real‑time instrument design

    Ardverium

    Seven interactive WebGL instruments for silicon — a wafer under a lamp, an FDTD wave field, a 32k‑agent layout router, a traced optics bench, and a chip package you can open. Physics first, art direction second.

    Role
    Concept, engineering, GPU performance
    Stack
    Raw WebGL 2 · GLSL ES 3.00 · Three.js r186 · custom TAA · no build step
    Scale
    — LOC across 7 instruments
    Target
    GeForce GT 730 @ 30 Hz — and every MacBook, by construction

    The through‑line

    • Real solvers, not shaders that look like solvers. FDTD leapfrog on a 9‑point Laplacian; GPGPU boids with a negotiated‑congestion A* router; GPU‑traced caustics with Snell, Fresnel and TIR through the actual glass; a full Airy thin‑film reflectance model with CIE 1931 integration.
    • One shared temporal AA engine (— LOC, verified byte‑identical across all 4 designs by MD5) with Halton jitter, motion vectors, a reactive mask and an output‑density ladder that steps 2 → 1.5 → 1.25 → 1 under budget pressure.
    • Every design has a CPU twin. The prism lab falls back to a genuine software ray tracer in a worker pool; the chip explorer falls back to a Canvas 2D perspective renderer with depth sorting and picking. Neither fallback is a static image.
    • Honest scope in the copy. The optics are illustrative art direction; the README says so plainly, and the production GLSL is verified offline by compiling it through surfaceless EGL and rendering the real frames.

  5. Model training

    LoRA pilot

    A from‑scratch LoRA trainer for a 27B model, built against the exact served quantised file, with the contamination controls written as enforceable code rather than a policy document.

    Role
    Design and implementation
    Stack
    Python · PyTorch · transformers · GGUF · llama.cpp · Yosys/Verilator/SymbiYosys
    Scale
    — LOC trainer, — LOC in — test files
    Status
    Held on a keep‑alive latch, not started

    How it stays clean

    • Hold‑outs never enter training. Every prompt, reference and target is checked by code for 15‑gram code overlap, 13‑gram prose overlap, repo blocklist with fork matching and AST hash. A flagged item is dropped and logged. An unset or empty manifest is a stop, never a skipped check.
    • No closed-model text. Rows may contain licence‑clean verbatim source, structured fields, self‑generated model text, or user templates. Nothing written by a proprietary model enters the data.
    • Exact runtime match. Sampling uses the pinned image digest and the benchmark's own argv; only port, slot count, temperature and seed may deviate.
    • Provenance per row. Seed → task → attempt → verification result → training row, with tool versions, model identity and engine identity, appended as JSONL.

  6. Evaluation · 27 models scored

    Regulatory translation benchmark

    A translation of Swedish nuclear‑safety regulations into English, and a scoring harness that compares 27 models on it — with the reference problem handled head‑on instead of hidden.

    Role
    Scoring methodology, harness, comparative analysis
    Stack
    Python · Jupyter · COMET‑22 / COMET‑QE · sacrebleu · multi‑reference scoring
    Scope
    2 editions (2018:1 and 2026:4) · 27 model outputs · 304 chunks
    Output
    Scored leaderboard, difference reports, a model debate, HTML/MD/PDF reports

    The methodological point

    • The Claude reference is a pseudo‑reference written under the models' own prompt rules, so reference‑based scores against it reward shared conventions as well as translation. The report says this out loud, then publishes an equal‑footing table where every model and the reference are scored against the same two external references.
    • Composite is a declared formula — 0.40 COMET‑22, 0.20 chrF++, 0.20 number F1, 0.10 terminology, 0.10 cleanliness — with source checks for Swedish residue, untranslated passages and length outliers.
    • The conclusion rests on side‑by‑side review rather than on the automatic scores; the report says that too.

    On equal footing, two open models outscore the Claude pseudo‑reference (92.2 and 92.1 vs 92.0). The scoring that favours the reference is the scoring that was reported first.

  7. Data integrity

    Origo Backup

    Encrypted incremental backup of two Linux machines to Proton Drive, with content‑defined deduplication written from first principles and a fresh‑machine restore path that is exercised, not assumed.

    Role
    Architecture and implementation
    Stack
    Python 3 stdlib · cryptography · AES‑256‑GCM · SQLite · vanilla JS web UI
    Scale
    — LOC across — files
    Protects
    2 systems over SSH · 2.05 M files / 126 GB · 91 tests passing

    What makes it hold up

    • The storage layout is the hard part, and it was derived, not chosen. 4 MiB content‑defined blocks packed into ~64 MiB encrypted packs, bucketed across folders to fit Proton Drive's 32,767‑entry folder limit — a limit the first live run hit, then designed around, then replaced with a pack layout whose listing cost was measured cold and warm before being accepted.
    • Remote sources stream, they don't mount. Oden is backed up over SSH by a worker that runs there, so no credentials are used on the remote; root scans are sudoised behind an askpass prompt, owner and setuid metadata are preserved by a separate root‑apply restore script, and snapshot‑as‑blocks means unchanged trees dedupe away entirely.
    • Security posture is default‑deny. AES‑256‑GCM with HMAC‑derived key separation, a loopback‑only web UI, a per‑launch API token with Host/Origin checks, and a recovery‑key import that restores onto a fresh machine.
    • Every fix lands with its diagnosis written down. The two dated FIXES documents describe the folder‑limit repair, the listing‑timeout diagnosis with measured times, and the retry/backoff ladders — the same verdict‑first style as the rest of this page.

Research & engineering notebooks

Modelling work where the sources are cited, the assumptions are explicit, and a result that does not pay is reported as a result that does not pay.

District heat, grid electricity, and thermoelectrics

A decision study for 10 km of heat at 5.66 MW: water grid against overhead line against a thermoelectric chain, with exergy, hydraulic loss, LMTD dry cooling and SPB carrier optimisation modelled in one notebook. Twenty‑four built‑in checks, twelve sourced references, and a stated modelling limit — it is not a vendor‑certified design.

The optimised SPB geometry returns −2.37 W net for 10 kW of heat. The answer was that it does not work, and that is the useful output.

Terrestrial conversion from a space reactor

NASA Kilopower and KRUSTY reworked into a ground conversion skid: a 6 kW electric thermal demonstrator, a dry‑cooled skid, a 3‑D finite‑element thermal model over a Delaunay mesh, a cooling‑failure transient, 72 CAD artefacts, and a seven‑stage commercialisation plan with real funding instruments named against each stage.

No reactor core, fuel, neutronics, shielding or nuclear transient is modelled. Thermal source power is an external boundary condition, and the notebook says so in its docstring.

Standard Model mass analysis

Geometric, harmonic and logarithmic structure in the lepton masses, with the Koide relation reproduced to 1.4 × 10−6 and the τ mass predicted from the electron, muon and Q = 2/3 to 0.43 quoted uncertainties.

Fixing the phase and fitting the electron predicts the muon 451.7σ away. The notebook reports that failure in the same voice as the success.

A physics programme under pre‑registration

Clifford algebra, G2 structures, octonion classification and Hasse diagrams, carried through dozens of documents with falsifiable claims pre‑registered, no‑go results kept as separate papers, and an open‑questions register with dated corrections. Parallel editions exist per model so a correction can be traced to the run that produced it.

30,361 lines of Markdown and 19,270 of Python, organised so that a prediction and its refutation are the same kind of artefact.

Practice

How the work is done — the constraints that produced it.

One append‑only decision log

2,683 entries recording what was decided, why, and who signed it off — from the frozen‑task rule to the comparability rule, to the measurement that OMP thread count was costing 97% of throughput on one model. It is the closest thing here to a primary source.

Measurement before belief

Every claim on this page traces to a file, a log, a benchmark row or a measurement. Where a number is an estimate, it is marked. Where a result was negative, it is stated as a negative result.

Independent review, in writing

Critique documents written by a separate reviewer, verdicts issued (DONE / PARTLY / NOT DONE), and the fixes applied in the open. Two design reviews in this portfolio each end with a full second document written against the first.

Licence hygiene

SPDX allow‑lists on training data and dependencies, explicit exclusions for non‑commercial and copyleft corpora, MIT and Apache notices shipped with every bundle, and self‑hosted fonts so nothing phones home.
